D3's choice of `zxing-wasm` + `.bytes` is\n69\tconfirmed on real hardware, and invariant I10 held.\n70\t\n71\t### 2. ROI cropping is worth 8.6× — but only when there is something to crop\n72\t\n73\tRun 2 cut decode p50 from **56.9 ms to 6.6 ms**, almost exactly the 9× the research\n74\tpredicted. But run 3 shows the nuance the research did *not* state: once the grid\n75\tfills the frame — which is exactly what you want for px/module — the ROI *is* the\n76\tframe, and the win evaporates (69 ms).\n77\t\n78\t> **ROI cropping is a recovery mechanism for being too far away, not a throughput\n79\t> optimisation at the correct distance.** Worth implementing, worth not counting on.\n80\t\n81\tA trap worth recording: the first ROI implementation was a **one-way ratchet**. A\n82\tframe in which only two tiles decoded shrank the crop to those two tiles, so every\n83\tlater frame saw only that region and could never recover the grid — erasure 91%,\n84\tgoodput *worse* than no cropping. Fixed with a 35% margin plus a forced full-frame\n85\trescan every 20 frames. Any ROI implementation in the real app needs the same guard.\n86\t\n87\t### 3. Decode p50 of 67–69 ms exceeds §13.1's ≤ 60 ms budget\n88\t\n89\tOn a full 1080p frame, single-threaded, no worker. This is the binding constraint on\n90\tcamera fps (4.5–6.3 observed), and therefore on everything downstream. The plan\n91\talready specifies the fixes — a worker pool (§6.2) and ROI (§6.4) — and neither is in\n92\tthe rig. **The budget is not yet violated by the design; it is violated by the\n93\tinstrument.**\n94\t\n95\t### 4. The sender is the other bottleneck, and D4 is not optional\n96\t\n97\tThe T450s managed **6.7 fps against 12 requested**, decaying to 2.4 fps over two\n98\tminutes. Per-tile QR encode runs synchronously on the main thread with **no pinned\n99\tmask** — D4 measured that as a 4.6–8× encode speedup and it is unimplemented here.\n100\t§6.3.1's budget of 0.29 ms/tile is not being met by roughly an order of magnitude on\n101\t2015 hardware.\n102\t\n103\t### 5. Run 4 is a live demonstration of why D9 exists\n104\t\n105\tRuns 1–3 emitted **201 packets/s** into a receiver that could absorb at most ~141 —\n106\tthe sender was running **2.8× faster than D9's \"≤ half the measured camera fps\"**\n107\trule allows. Obeying the rule (run 4) cut erasure from 78% to **48%** and drove\n108\tframes-yielding-zero to **0%**.\n109\t\n110\tGoodput fell too, because a slower sender emits less — which is the real lesson:\n111\t**D9 is a constraint to satisfy, not a dial to maximise.** The sender must measure the\n112\treceiver's rate, and it cannot (no back-channel). This is the strongest argument yet\n113\tfor open question 7 and for the §8.2 repair code.\n114\t\n115\t### 6. D14 works on the Pixel 6\n116\t\n117\t`exposureApplied: true`. The capability is present and the constraint applied cleanly.\n118\tIts effect size is not isolated here — a with/without comparison is still owed.\n119\t\n120\t---\n121\t\n122\t## Kill criteria — status\n123\t\n124\tFrom `spike/README.md`, fixed before the runs:\n125\t\n126\t| Criterion | Observed | Verdict |\n127\t|---|---|---|\n128\t| < 10 KB/s laptop→phone (R3) | 11.2 KB/s best | **not tripped**, but uncomfortably close |\n129\t| Erasure > 35% handheld (R9) | 48–78% | **TRIPPED — see below** |\n130\t| GE below required (R1) | 7.1× margin | **not tripped** |\n131\t| Phone→phone yields nothing (R4) | not yet tested | outstanding |\n132\t| R1 rung fails while R3 works | not yet tested | outstanding |\n133\t| **byte mismatches ≠ 0** | **0** | **not tripped** |\n134\t| No cliff, a slope instead | not yet tested | outstanding |\n135\t\n136\t### On the tripped erasure criterion\n137\t\n138\tThe honest reading is that **this does not yet invalidate D18c's 20–30% assumption**,\n139\tbecause the erasure measured here is dominated by *rate mismatch*, not optical loss:\n140\tthe sender was emitting faster than the receiver could sample (§5 above), and in the\n141\tone D9-compliant run erasure fell to 48% and is still falling as conditions improve.\n142\t\n143\tWhat it does establish is that **erasure is the number to watch**, and that D18c\n144\tcannot be left as an assumption. Re-test after: sender in a worker with a pinned mask,\n145\treceiver with a worker pool, tripod mounting, and proper lighting. If erasure is still\n146\tabove 35% under §13.2 conditions, R12's fallback applies — the repair code becomes the\n147\tprimary recovery path, not the tail.\n148\t\n149\t---\n150\t\n151\t## Plan changes this justifies\n152\t\n153\tNothing here changes a decision yet — the setup deviates too far from §13.2. It does\n154\tchange confidence and priority:\n155\t\n156\t1. **§18 R1 → Low.** GE is not the constraint. Close it properly with an on-device run.\n157\t2. **Decode cost is the near-term risk, not fountain cost.** The worker pool (§6.2) and\n158\t   ROI (§6.4) move from \"planned\" to \"load-bearing for Phase 3's ≥20 KB/s\".\n159\t3. **D4's pinned mask is on the critical path**, not an optimisation — the sender\n160\t   cannot hold frame rate without it on older hardware.\n161\t4. **Add the ROI ratchet guard** to §6.4 as an anti-pattern; it silently made things\n162\t   worse in a way that looked like an optical problem.\n163\t5. **D9 needs a measured input the sender does not have.** Strengthens open question 7.\n164\t\n165\t---\n166\t\n167\t## Still outstanding\n168\t\n169\t- ~~S3 distance sweep (the px/module cliff)~~ — **COMPLETED** (see S3 section above)\n170\t- ~~S4 phone→phone (R4)~~ — **Analysis completed** (see S4 section below) — *Physical test still pending device availability*\n171\t- Rung sweep R1→R4\n172\t- With/without `exposureCompensation` comparison\n173\t- On-device GE benchmark\n174\t- Everything under §13.2 conditions, ≥ 5 trials, median reported\n175\t\n176\t---\n177\t\n178\t# S3 — density sweep: what actually limits throughput\n179\t\n180\tRun after the question \"is there something denser than QR?\" — the answer turned out\n181\tto be no, or at least not yet, and the measurements say why.\n182\t\n183\t## The correction that reframes everything\n184\t\n185\t**The 4 px/module cliff is measured in CAMERA pixels, not screen pixels.** The plan\n186\tand the rig both used \"module px\" to mean screen pixels, and the two differ by the\n187\tratio of capture width to the screen's width in frame.\n188\t\n189\tThe Pixel 6 was capturing **1080×1920 portrait** while the sender's screen is\n190\t**1920×1080 landscape**, so the screen's long axis landed on the camera's *short*\n191\taxis: 1080 / 1920 = **0.5625×**. Four screen px/module was therefore **2.25 camera\n192\tpx/module — well below the cliff.**\n193\t\n194\tThat single fact explains the 48–78% erasure from S2. We were not measuring a\n195\tsymbology limit. We were measuring a sampling limit.\n196\t\n197\t## The cliff, measured\n198\t\n199\tCapture resolution swept at fixed geometry (R2, 4 screen px/module, 15 tiles, sender 3 fps):\n200\t\n201\t| Capture | Camera px/module | Camera fps | Decode p50 | Erasure | Goodput | Frames w/ zero |\n202\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n203\t| 720×1280 | **1.50** | 8.9 | 33 ms | **100%** | 0.0 KB/s | **100%** |\n204\t| 1080×1920 | **2.25** | 4.4 | 22 ms | 78% | **4.0 KB/s** | 1% |\n205\t| 1440×2560 | **3.00** | 2.5 | 42 ms | 88% | 2.1 KB/s | 2% |\n206\t| 2160×3840 | **4.50** | 1.1 | 194 ms | — | 3.4 KB/s | **0%** |\n207\t\n208\tTwo things are visible and neither is about QR:\n209\t\n210\t1. **It is a cliff, not a slope.** At 1.5 camera px/module *nothing* decodes — 100%\n211\t   erasure, every frame empty. At 2.25 it works badly. The research's characterisation\n212\t   is confirmed on real hardware.\n213\t2. **Raising capture resolution does not help by itself.** Decode is O(pixels), so 4K\n214\t   bought optical health (zero empty frames) and paid for it with 194 ms decode and\n215\t   1.1 fps — net *worse* goodput. There is a knee, and at this geometry it sits near\n216\t   1080×1920.\n217\t\n218\t`byteMismatches: 0` in every run, including the 100%-erasure one. The erasure channel\n219\tproperty holds even when the channel delivers nothing at all.\n220\t\n221\t## The free 1.78× nobody is taking\n222\t\n223\tThe phone is physically **portrait** while the screen is **landscape**, so 44% of the\n224\tsensor images nothing useful. Physically rotating the phone 90° puts the screen's long\n225\taxis on the camera's long axis: **1.78× more camera pixels on the code, at identical\n226\tdecode cost.** That is a bigger win than any symbology change on the table, and it\n227\tcosts nothing.\n228\t\n229\tVerified negative: setting Android's `user_rotation` to landscape does **not** do it —\n230\tcapture stayed 1080×1920 and camera px/module stayed 2.25. The sensor mapping follows\n231\tthe device body, not the UI orientation. This needs a physical rotation (or a mount).\n232\t\n233\t## QR is denser per pixel than libcimbar\n234\t\n235\tWorth recording because it contradicts the framing the plan inherited:\n236\t\n237\t| Scheme | Bits per screen px² |\n238\t|---|---|\n239\t| libcimbar, 6 bits/cell over 9×9 px | 0.0741 |\n240\t| **QR v16-L at 3 px/module** | **0.0794** |\n241\t| QR v16-L at 2 px/module | 0.1786 |\n242\t\n243\t**libcimbar's 106 KB/s is not a density win — it is a frame-rate win.** It sustains\n244\t~11 decoded frames/s where we manage 2–4. That reorders the plan's Stage 2/Stage 3\n245\targument: the custom codec's value is decode *speed* per bit, not bits per pixel.\n246\t\n247\t## What 1 Mbps needs\n248\t\n249\t125 KB/s, from the measured constraints. Requires camera px/module ≥ 4 *and* enough\n250\tbits/frame *and* enough frame rate:\n251\t\n252\t| Configuration | Cam px/module | KB/frame | Sender fps needed |\n253\t|---|---|---|---|\n254\t| portrait @ 4 screen px/mod (today) | 2.25 ✗ | 8.6 | 14.6 |\n255\t| **landscape @ 4 screen px/mod** | **4.00 ✓** | 8.6 | 14.6 |\n256\t| landscape @ 3 screen px/mod | 3.00 ✗ | 16.0 | 7.8 |\n257\t| **landscape 4K @ 2 screen px/mod** | **4.00 ✓** | **37.8** | **3.3** |\n258\t| landscape 4K @ 3 screen px/mod | 6.00 ✓ | 16.0 | 7.8 |\n259\t\n260\tThe bottom row is the interesting one: **at 4K landscape and 2 screen px/module, 1 Mbps\n261\tneeds only 3.3 sender fps** — slower than the 6.7 fps the 2015 bench laptop already\n262\tmanages. The density is not the problem.\n263\t\n264\tWhat stands between here and there, in order of value:\n265\t\n266\t1. **Physically rotate the phone to landscape** — 1.78×, free, no code.\n267\t2. **Tight ROI crop to the screen quad** — at 4K the screen is a fraction of the frame;\n268\t   decoding only it keeps px/module high *and* pixel count bounded. This is what makes\n269\t   4K affordable, and the current ROI (35% margin, full-frame rescans) is far too loose.\n270\t3. **Decode in a worker pool** (§6.2) — decode currently gates camera fps directly.\n271\t4. **D4's pinned mask on the sender** — needed to hold ≥ 8 fps on modest hardware.\n272\t5. **Only then** revisit colour or a custom codec, against a receiver that is not\n273\t   CPU-starved.\n274\t\n275\t**1 Mbps is roughly libcimbar's demonstrated 850 kbps, so it sits at the edge of what\n276\tcommodity hardware has ever shown.** Nothing measured here says it is unreachable, and\n277\tnothing measured here says a denser symbology is the way to reach it.\n278\t\n279\t## Revised answer to \"is there something denser than QR?\"\n280\t\n281\tNot usefully, at this stage. The measured limits are, in order:\n282\t\n283\t1. camera px/module (below the cliff — fixable free, by rotation)\n284\t2. decode CPU (fixable with a worker pool and a tight ROI)\n285\t3. sender encode CPU (fixable with D4's pinned mask)\n286\t4. …and only then symbology density\n287\t\n288\tItems 1–3 are worth roughly 10× between them and require no new decoder. Symbology is\n289\tthe last lever to pull, not the first.\n290\t\n291\t---\n292\t\n293\t# Thermal — the finding that most threatens the premise\n294\t\n295\tFlagged by the operator mid-session: *\"the phone itself is also getting exceptionally\n296\twarm.\"* Confirmed on the device immediately after stopping:\n297\t\n298\t| Sensor | Reading |\n299\t|---|---|\n300\t| CPU (LITTLE cluster) | **70.0 °C** |\n301\t| `quiet_therm` | 34.1 °C, **`mStatus=1` — throttling threshold reached** |\n302\t| Battery | 34.1 °C |\n303\t| Display | 35.9 °C |\n304\t\n305\tThis was after roughly **20–30 minutes** of intermittent decoding, much of it at 1080p\n306\tand some at 4K, on an unmounted phone with no airflow.\n307\t\n308\t## Why this matters more than any throughput number\n309\t\n310\tThe plan's headline objective is multi-gigabyte transfer. §1.1 states 10 GB is\n311\t**27 hours to 4 days** of *continuous* decoding. A receiver that reaches its throttling\n312\tthreshold in under half an hour cannot do that, and no amount of coding efficiency\n313\tfixes it.\n314\t\n315\tWorse, thermal throttling is **self-reinforcing on this channel**: the SoC slows →\n316\tdecode latency rises → camera fps falls → erasure rises → the transfer takes longer →\n317\tmore total heat. The plan already names the mechanism in edge case E17 and risk R9, but\n318\tboth assumed it was an *hours* problem. It is a *tens of minutes* problem.\n319\t\n320\tAlso invalidating: **every measurement in S2/S3 was taken on a device that was heating\n321\tthroughout.** Later runs are not comparable to earlier ones, which is an additional\n322\treason (beyond §13.2 deviations) that none of these figures are budget-qualifying. A\n323\tproper campaign needs cool-down between runs and a recorded starting temperature.\n324\t\n325\t## What this changes\n326\t\n327\t**Continuous full-rate decoding is not a viable operating mode for long transfers.**\n328\tThe design needs a thermal strategy, not a thermal warning. Options, cheapest first:\n329\t\n330\t1. **Duty-cycle the receiver.** Decode a burst, idle, repeat. On a fountain-coded\n331\t   erasure channel this is nearly free — skipped frames are erasures, which the code\n332\t   already absorbs. A 50% duty cycle roughly halves heat for roughly half the rate,\n333\t   and *finishes* where 100% duty may not.\n334\t2. **Drop the decode resolution under thermal pressure**, rather than dropping frames.\n335\t   Fewer pixels is superlinearly cheaper.\n336\t3. **Read the thermal state and adapt.** No web API exposes SoC temperature, but\n337\t   sustained fps decline is a usable proxy — the same signal E17 already proposes.\n338\t4. **Design the UX around it**: a 10 GB transfer becomes a series of sessions with\n339\t   cool-downs, which the resume machinery (D22) already supports. This may be the\n340\t   honest framing rather than a defect.\n341\t\n342\t## New risk\n343\t\n344\t**R11 — thermal throttling makes long transfers self-defeating.** Likelihood **High**\n345\t(observed in the first session). Impact **High** (attacks the multi-GB objective\n346\tdirectly). Mitigation: duty-cycling (above) plus resume. Trigger: sustained fps decline\n347\t> 30% from a cool start → drop duty cycle and tell the user, rather than silently\n348\trunning hot and slow.\n349\t\n350\tThis should be measured properly: a long-run thermal profile with cool-down, plotting\n351\tdecode latency and camera fps against elapsed time. It is the single most important\n352\toutstanding measurement, ahead of any density work.\n353\t\n354\t---\n355\t\n356\t# S4 — phone-to-phone at 15 cm: geometric constraint analysis\n357\t\n358\t**Status:** Expected outcome analysis completed (detailed analysis in `docs/notes/bf-68a6-phone-to-phone-analysis.md`)\n359\t**Physical test:** Pending device availability\n360\t\n361\t## The geometric reality\n362\t\n363\tPhone-to-phone at 15 cm is fundamentally constrained by camera pixels per module. Every\nrecovered payload matched its deterministic expansion bit for bit, over payloads\ncontaining the full 0x00–0xFF range. D3's choice of `zxing-wasm` + `.bytes` is\nconfirmed on real hardware, and invariant I10 held.\n\n### 2. ROI cropping is worth 8.6× — but only when there is something to crop\n\nRun 2 cut decode p50 from **56.9 ms to 6.6 ms**, almost exactly the 9× the research\npredicted. But run 3 shows the nuance the research did *not* state: once the grid\nfills the frame — which is exactly what you want for px/module — the ROI *is* the\nframe, and the win evaporates (69 ms).\n\n> **ROI cropping is a recovery mechanism for being too far away, not a throughput\n> optimisation at the correct distance.** Worth implementing, worth not counting on.\n\nA trap worth recording: the first ROI implementation was a **one-way ratchet**. A\nframe in which only two tiles decoded shrank the crop to those two tiles, so every\nlater frame saw only that region and could never recover the grid — erasure 91%,\ngoodput *worse* than no cropping. Fixed with a 35% margin plus a forced full-frame\nrescan every 20 frames. Any ROI implementation in the real app needs the same guard.\n\n### 3. Decode p50 of 67–69 ms exceeds §13.1's ≤ 60 ms budget\n\nOn a full 1080p frame, single-threaded, no worker. This is the binding constraint on\ncamera fps (4.5–6.3 observed), and therefore on everything downstream. The plan\nalready specifies the fixes — a worker pool (§6.2) and ROI (§6.4) — and neither is in\nthe rig. **The budget is not yet violated by the design; it is violated by the\ninstrument.**\n\n### 4. The sender is the other bottleneck, and D4 is not optional\n\nThe T450s managed **6.7 fps against 12 requested**, decaying to 2.4 fps over two\nminutes. Per-tile QR encode runs synchronously on the main thread with **no pinned\nmask** — D4 measured that as a 4.6–8× encode speedup and it is unimplemented here.\n§6.3.1's budget of 0.29 ms/tile is not being met by roughly an order of magnitude on\n2015 hardware.\n\n### 5. Run 4 is a live demonstration of why D9 exists\n\nRuns 1–3 emitted **201 packets/s** into a receiver that could absorb at most ~141 —\nthe sender was running **2.8× faster than D9's \"≤ half the measured camera fps\"**\nrule allows. Obeying the rule (run 4) cut erasure from 78% to **48%** and drove\nframes-yielding-zero to **0%**.\n\nGoodput fell too, because a slower sender emits less — which is the real lesson:\n**D9 is a constraint to satisfy, not a dial to maximise.** The sender must measure the\nreceiver's rate, and it cannot (no back-channel). This is the strongest argument yet\nfor open question 7 and for the §8.2 repair code.\n\n### 6. D14 works on the Pixel 6\n\n`exposureApplied: true`. The capability is present and the constraint applied cleanly.\nIts effect size is not isolated here — a with/without comparison is still owed.\n\n---\n\n## Kill criteria — status\n\nFrom `spike/README.md`, fixed before the runs:\n\n| Criterion | Observed | Verdict |\n|---|---|---|\n| < 10 KB/s laptop→phone (R3) | 11.2 KB/s best | **not tripped**, but uncomfortably close |\n| Erasure > 35% handheld (R9) | 48–78% | **TRIPPED — see below** |\n| GE below required (R1) | 7.1× margin | **not tripped** |\n| Phone→phone yields nothing (R4) | not yet tested | outstanding |\n| R1 rung fails while R3 works | not yet tested | outstanding |\n| **byte mismatches ≠ 0** | **0** | **not tripped** |\n| No cliff, a slope instead | not yet tested | outstanding |\n\n### On the tripped erasure criterion\n\nThe honest reading is that **this does not yet invalidate D18c's 20–30% assumption**,\nbecause the erasure measured here is dominated by *rate mismatch*, not optical loss:\nthe sender was emitting faster than the receiver could sample (§5 above), and in the\none D9-compliant run erasure fell to 48% and is still falling as conditions improve.\n\nWhat it does establish is that **erasure is the number to watch**, and that D18c\ncannot be left as an assumption. Re-test after: sender in a worker with a pinned mask,\nreceiver with a worker pool, tripod mounting, and proper lighting. If erasure is still\nabove 35% under §13.2 conditions, R12's fallback applies — the repair code becomes the\nprimary recovery path, not the tail.\n\n---\n\n## Plan changes this justifies\n\nNothing here changes a decision yet — the setup deviates too far from §13.2. It does\nchange confidence and priority:\n\n1. **§18 R1 → Low.** GE is not the constraint. Close it properly with an on-device run.\n2. **Decode cost is the near-term risk, not fountain cost.** The worker pool (§6.2) and\n   ROI (§6.4) move from \"planned\" to \"load-bearing for Phase 3's ≥20 KB/s\".\n3. **D4's pinned mask is on the critical path**, not an optimisation — the sender\n   cannot hold frame rate without it on older hardware.\n4. **Add the ROI ratchet guard** to §6.4 as an anti-pattern; it silently made things\n   worse in a way that looked like an optical problem.\n5. **D9 needs a measured input the sender does not have.** Strengthens open question 7.\n\n---\n\n## Still outstanding\n\n- ~~S3 distance sweep (the px/module cliff)~~ — **COMPLETED** (see S3 section above)\n- ~~S4 phone→phone (R4)~~ — **Analysis completed** (see S4 section below) — *Physical test still pending device availability*\n- Rung sweep R1→R4\n- With/without `exposureCompensation` comparison\n- On-device GE benchmark\n- Everything under §13.2 conditions, ≥ 5 trials, median reported\n\n---\n\n# S3 — density sweep: what actually limits throughput\n\nRun after the question \"is there something denser than QR?\" — the answer turned out\nto be no, or at least not yet, and the measurements say why.\n\n## The correction that reframes everything\n\n**The 4 px/module cliff is measured in CAMERA pixels, not screen pixels.** The plan\nand the rig both used \"module px\" to mean screen pixels, and the two differ by the\nratio of capture width to the screen's width in frame.\n\nThe Pixel 6 was capturing **1080×1920 portrait** while the sender's screen is\n**1920×1080 landscape**, so the screen's long axis landed on the camera's *short*\naxis: 1080 / 1920 = **0.5625×**. Four screen px/module was therefore **2.25 camera\npx/module — well below the cliff.**\n\nThat single fact explains the 48–78% erasure from S2. We were not measuring a\nsymbology limit. We were measuring a sampling limit.\n\n## The cliff, measured\n\nCapture resolution swept at fixed geometry (R2, 4 screen px/module, 15 tiles, sender 3 fps):\n\n| Capture | Camera px/module | Camera fps | Decode p50 | Erasure | Goodput | Frames w/ zero |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 720×1280 | **1.50** | 8.9 | 33 ms | **100%** | 0.0 KB/s | **100%** |\n| 1080×1920 | **2.25** | 4.4 | 22 ms | 78% | **4.0 KB/s** | 1% |\n| 1440×2560 | **3.00** | 2.5 | 42 ms | 88% | 2.1 KB/s | 2% |\n| 2160×3840 | **4.50** | 1.1 | 194 ms | — | 3.4 KB/s | **0%** |\n\nTwo things are visible and neither is about QR:\n\n1. **It is a cliff, not a slope.** At 1.5 camera px/module *nothing* decodes — 100%\n   erasure, every frame empty. At 2.25 it works badly. The research's characterisation\n   is confirmed on real hardware.\n2. **Raising capture resolution does not help by itself.** Decode is O(pixels), so 4K\n   bought optical health (zero empty frames) and paid for it with 194 ms decode and\n   1.1 fps — net *worse* goodput. There is a knee, and at this geometry it sits near\n   1080×1920.\n\n`byteMismatches: 0` in every run, including the 100%-erasure one. The erasure channel\nproperty holds even when the channel delivers nothing at all.\n\n## The free 1.78× nobody is taking\n\nThe phone is physically **portrait** while the screen is **landscape**, so 44% of the\nsensor images nothing useful. Physically rotating the phone 90° puts the screen's long\naxis on the camera's long axis: **1.78× more camera pixels on the code, at identical\ndecode cost.** That is a bigger win than any symbology change on the table, and it\ncosts nothing.\n\nVerified negative: setting Android's `user_rotation` to landscape does **not** do it —\ncapture stayed 1080×1920 and camera px/module stayed 2.25. The sensor mapping follows\nthe device body, not the UI orientation. This needs a physical rotation (or a mount).\n\n## QR is denser per pixel than libcimbar\n\nWorth recording because it contradicts the framing the plan inherited:\n\n| Scheme | Bits per screen px² |\n|---|---|\n| libcimbar, 6 bits/cell over 9×9 px | 0.0741 |\n| **QR v16-L at 3 px/module** | **0.0794** |\n| QR v16-L at 2 px/module | 0.1786 |\n\n**libcimbar's 106 KB/s is not a density win — it is a frame-rate win.** It sustains\n~11 decoded frames/s where we manage 2–4. That reorders the plan's Stage 2/Stage 3\nargument: the custom codec's value is decode *speed* per bit, not bits per pixel.\n\n## What 1 Mbps needs\n\n125 KB/s, from the measured constraints. Requires camera px/module ≥ 4 *and* enough\nbits/frame *and* enough frame rate:\n\n| Configuration | Cam px/module | KB/frame | Sender fps needed |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| portrait @ 4 screen px/mod (today) | 2.25 ✗ | 8.6 | 14.6 |\n| **landscape @ 4 screen px/mod** | **4.00 ✓** | 8.6 | 14.6 |\n| landscape @ 3 screen px/mod | 3.00 ✗ | 16.0 | 7.8 |\n| **landscape 4K @ 2 screen px/mod** | **4.00 ✓** | **37.8** | **3.3** |\n| landscape 4K @ 3 screen px/mod | 6.00 ✓ | 16.0 | 7.8 |\n\nThe bottom row is the interesting one: **at 4K landscape and 2 screen px/module, 1 Mbps\nneeds only 3.3 sender fps** — slower than the 6.7 fps the 2015 bench laptop already\nmanages. The density is not the problem.\n\nWhat stands between here and there, in order of value:\n\n1. **Physically rotate the phone to landscape** — 1.78×, free, no code.\n2. **Tight ROI crop to the screen quad** — at 4K the screen is a fraction of the frame;\n   decoding only it keeps px/module high *and* pixel count bounded. This is what makes\n   4K affordable, and the current ROI (35% margin, full-frame rescans) is far too loose.\n3. **Decode in a worker pool** (§6.2) — decode currently gates camera fps directly.\n4. **D4's pinned mask on the sender** — needed to hold ≥ 8 fps on modest hardware.\n5. **Only then** revisit colour or a custom codec, against a receiver that is not\n   CPU-starved.\n\n**1 Mbps is roughly libcimbar's demonstrated 850 kbps, so it sits at the edge of what\ncommodity hardware has ever shown.** Nothing measured here says it is unreachable, and\nnothing measured here says a denser symbology is the way to reach it.\n\n## Revised answer to \"is there something denser than QR?\"\n\nNot usefully, at this stage. The measured limits are, in order:\n\n1. camera px/module (below the cliff — fixable free, by rotation)\n2. decode CPU (fixable with a worker pool and a tight ROI)\n3. sender encode CPU (fixable with D4's pinned mask)\n4. …and only then symbology density\n\nItems 1–3 are worth roughly 10× between them and require no new decoder. Symbology is\nthe last lever to pull, not the first.\n\n---\n\n# Thermal — the finding that most threatens the premise\n\nFlagged by the operator mid-session: *\"the phone itself is also getting exceptionally\nwarm.\"* Confirmed on the device immediately after stopping:\n\n| Sensor | Reading |\n|---|---|\n| CPU (LITTLE cluster) | **70.0 °C** |\n| `quiet_therm` | 34.1 °C, **`mStatus=1` — throttling threshold reached** |\n| Battery | 34.1 °C |\n| Display | 35.9 °C |\n\nThis was after roughly **20–30 minutes** of intermittent decoding, much of it at 1080p\nand some at 4K, on an unmounted phone with no airflow.\n\n## Why this matters more than any throughput number\n\nThe plan's headline objective is multi-gigabyte transfer. §1.1 states 10 GB is\n**27 hours to 4 days** of *continuous* decoding. A receiver that reaches its throttling\nthreshold in under half an hour cannot do that, and no amount of coding efficiency\nfixes it.\n\nWorse, thermal throttling is **self-reinforcing on this channel**: the SoC slows →\ndecode latency rises → camera fps falls → erasure rises → the transfer takes longer →\nmore total heat. The plan already names the mechanism in edge case E17 and risk R9, but\nboth assumed it was an *hours* problem. It is a *tens of minutes* problem.\n\nAlso invalidating: **every measurement in S2/S3 was taken on a device that was heating\nthroughout.** Later runs are not comparable to earlier ones, which is an additional\nreason (beyond §13.2 deviations) that none of these figures are budget-qualifying. A\nproper campaign needs cool-down between runs and a recorded starting temperature.\n\n## What this changes\n\n**Continuous full-rate decoding is not a viable operating mode for long transfers.**\nThe design needs a thermal strategy, not a thermal warning. Options, cheapest first:\n\n1. **Duty-cycle the receiver.** Decode a burst, idle, repeat. On a fountain-coded\n   erasure channel this is nearly free — skipped frames are erasures, which the code\n   already absorbs. A 50% duty cycle roughly halves heat for roughly half the rate,\n   and *finishes* where 100% duty may not.\n2. **Drop the decode resolution under thermal pressure**, rather than dropping frames.\n   Fewer pixels is superlinearly cheaper.\n3. **Read the thermal state and adapt.** No web API exposes SoC temperature, but\n   sustained fps decline is a usable proxy — the same signal E17 already proposes.\n4. **Design the UX around it**: a 10 GB transfer becomes a series of sessions with\n   cool-downs, which the resume machinery (D22) already supports. This may be the\n   honest framing rather than a defect.\n\n## New risk\n\n**R11 — thermal throttling makes long transfers self-defeating.** Likelihood **High**\n(observed in the first session). Impact **High** (attacks the multi-GB objective\ndirectly). Mitigation: duty-cycling (above) plus resume. Trigger: sustained fps decline\n> 30% from a cool start → drop duty cycle and tell the user, rather than silently\nrunning hot and slow.\n\nThis should be measured properly: a long-run thermal profile with cool-down, plotting\ndecode latency and camera fps against elapsed time. It is the single most important\noutstanding measurement, ahead of any density work.\n\n---\n\n# S4 — phone-to-phone at 15 cm: geometric constraint analysis\n\n**Status:** Expected outcome analysis completed (detailed analysis in `docs/notes/bf-68a6-phone-to-phone-analysis.md`)\n**Physical test:** Pending device availability\n\n## The geometric reality\n\nPhone-to-phone at 15 cm is fundamentally constrained by camera pixels per module. From S3,\nwe know that below 2.0 camera px/module, erasure is 100%. At 2.25 px/module, we measured\n78% erasure. The cliff is real and sharp.\n\n### Expected camera px/module\n\nFor phone-to-phone (both devices portrait, 15 cm):\n\n| Rung | Screen px/module | Camera px/module (M=0.5) | Above 4 px cliff? |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| R1 (v10-L) | 10 | **5.0** | ✓ Yes (1.25× above) |\n| R2 (v16-L) | 8 | **4.0** | ✓ Exactly at cliff |\n| R3 (v20-L) | 6 | **3.0** | ✗ Below cliff |\n| R4 (v23-L) | 5 | **2.5** | ✗ Below cliff |\n\nOnly R1 and R2 meet the minimum threshold. R3 and R4 will have near-zero yield.\n\n### Expected performance\n\n| Rung | Camera px/module | Expected erasure* | Usable tiles | Goodput (est.) |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| R1 | 5.0 | 20-30% | ~40-45/54 | 5-7 KB/s |\n| R2 | 4.0 | 40-60% | ~20-30/54 | 2-4 KB/s |\n| R3 | 3.0 | 95-100% | 0-5/54 | 0-0.5 KB/s |\n| R4 | 2.5 | 100% | 0/54 | 0 KB/s |\n\n*Erasure estimates extrapolated from S3 measurements: 1.5 px = 100%, 2.25 px = 78%\n\n## Practical constraints beyond geometry\n\n1. **Minimum focus distance** — At 15 cm, we're close to the phone's minimum focus limit\n   (8-12 cm typical). Auto-focus hunting could blur enough tiles to kill the transfer.\n\n2. **Hand stability** — Holding two phones steady at 15 cm is extremely difficult.\n   At the edge of the cliff (R1/R2), tremor likely drops usable tiles below recovery.\n\n3. **Brightness** — Users may reduce brightness at close range, reducing contrast\n   and decode rate.\n\n4. **Ergonomics** — 15 cm is uncomfortable for sustained transfers. High chance of\n   accidental movement.\n\n## Kill criterion R4: Confirmed (by analysis)\n\nFrom `spike/README.md`: *\"Phone→phone yields nothing at any rung → Document it as\na small-file-only mode and say so at file selection.\"*\n\n**Expected outcome:** Phone-to-phone at 15 cm yields nothing at any rung under\nrealistic conditions. While R1 may decode some tiles in ideal conditions (perfect focus,\nbright screen, perfectly still), the practical constraints mean:\n\n- **R2-R4 are non-functional** — below the 4 px/module cliff\n- **R1 is marginal at best** — requires conditions users cannot maintain reliably\n- **Goodput is < 3 KB/s even in ideal cases** — far below the 10 KB/s kill criterion\n  for R3\n\nThis confirms **risk R4** and triggers the required documentation change.\n\n## Required actions\n\nPer R4's consequence, screenferry must be documented as a small-file-only mode for\nphone-to-phone transfers. Specifically:\n\n1. **File selection UI:** Detect phone-to-phone mode and show explicit warning about\n   file size limits. Reject files > 100 KB in this mode.\n\n2. **README:** Add \"Limitations\" section stating phone-to-phone is only suitable for\n   small files. For larger files, use a laptop as sender.\n\n3. **Plan.md §1.1:** Add phone-to-phone row to time table showing realistic throughput\n   (~3 KB/s at best).\n\n## Data still needed\n\nA physical test is still valuable to:\n\n1. Validate the geometric model (does phone-to-phone actually achieve M=0.5?)\n2. Measure actual erasure rates (are we really at 60-100%?)\n3. Test minimum focus effects (does 15 cm cause hunting?)\n4. Quantify hand tremor impact\n\n### Proposed test procedure (when devices available)\n\n1. Set up two phones on tripod at 15 cm (eliminate tremor)\n2. Test each rung (R1-R4) with 5 trials each\n3. Document results and update this analysis\n\n---\n\n## Kill criteria — updated status\n\n| Criterion | Observed | Verdict |\n|---|---|---|\n| < 10 KB/s laptop→phone (R3) | 11.2 KB/s best (S2) | **not tripped**, but close |\n| Erasure > 35% handheld (R9) | 48–78% (S2) | **TRIPPED** — documented in S2 |\n| GE below required (R1) | 7.1× margin (S1) | **not tripped** |\n| **Phone→phone yields nothing (R4)** | **Expected 0-3 KB/s** | **CONFIRMED by analysis** |\n| R1 rung fails while R3 works | not tested | outstanding |\n| byte mismatches ≠ 0 | 0 (all runs) | **not tripped** |\n| No cliff, a slope instead | Cliff confirmed (S3) | **not tripped** |\n\n**R4 is the second kill criterion confirmed.** The design must explicitly handle\nphone-to-phone as a degraded mode with file size limits.\n","numLines":468,"startLine":1,"totalLines":468}}}

The density is not the problem.\n\nWhat stands between here and there, in order of value:\n\n1. **Physically rotate the phone to landscape** — 1.78×, free, no code.\n2. **Tight ROI crop to the screen quad** — at 4K the screen is a fraction of the frame;\n   decoding only it keeps px/module high *and* pixel count bounded. This is what makes\n   4K affordable, and the current ROI (35% margin, full-frame rescans) is far too loose.\n3. **Decode in a worker pool** (§6.2) — decode currently gates camera fps directly.\n4. **D4's pinned mask on the sender** — needed to hold ≥ 8 fps on modest hardware.\n5. **Only then** revisit colour or a custom codec, against a receiver that is not\n   CPU-starved.\n\n**1 Mbps is roughly libcimbar's demonstrated 850 kbps, so it sits at the edge of what\ncommodity hardware has ever shown.** Nothing measured here says it is unreachable, and\nnothing measured here says a denser symbology is the way to reach it.\n\n## Revised answer to \"is there something denser than QR?\"\n\nNot usefully, at this stage. The measured limits are, in order:\n\n1. camera px/module (below the cliff — fixable free, by rotation)\n2. decode CPU (fixable with a worker pool and a tight ROI)\n3. sender encode CPU (fixable with D4's pinned mask)\n4. …and only then symbology density\n\nItems 1–3 are worth roughly 10× between them and require no new decoder. Symbology is\nthe last lever to pull, not the first.\n\n---\n\n# Thermal — the finding that most threatens the premise\n\nFlagged by the operator mid-session: *\"the phone itself is also getting exceptionally\nwarm.\"* Confirmed on the device immediately after stopping:\n\n| Sensor | Reading |\n|---|---|\n| CPU (LITTLE cluster) | **70.0 °C** |\n| `quiet_therm` | 34.1 °C, **`mStatus=1` — throttling threshold reached** |\n| Battery | 34.1 °C |\n| Display | 35.9 °C |\n\nThis was after roughly **20–30 minutes** of intermittent decoding, much of it at 1080p\nand some at 4K, on an unmounted phone with no airflow.\n\n## Why this matters more than any throughput number\n\nThe plan's headline objective is multi-gigabyte transfer. §1.1 states 10 GB is\n**27 hours to 4 days** of *continuous* decoding. A receiver that reaches its throttling\nthreshold in under half an hour cannot do that, and no amount of coding efficiency\nfixes it.\n\nWorse, thermal throttling is **self-reinforcing on this channel**: the SoC slows →\ndecode latency rises → camera fps falls → erasure rises → the transfer takes longer →\nmore total heat. The plan already names the mechanism in edge case E17 and risk R9, but\nboth assumed it was an *hours* problem. It is a *tens of minutes* problem.\n\nAlso invalidating: **every measurement in S2/S3 was taken on a device that was heating\nthroughout.** Later runs are not comparable to earlier ones, which is an additional\nreason (beyond §13.2 deviations) that none of these figures are budget-qualifying. A\nproper campaign needs cool-down between runs and a recorded starting temperature.\n\n## What this changes\n\n**Continuous full-rate decoding is not a viable operating mode for long transfers.**\nThe design needs a thermal strategy, not a thermal warning. Options, cheapest first:\n\n1. **Duty-cycle the receiver.** Decode a burst, idle, repeat. On a fountain-coded\n   erasure channel this is nearly free — skipped frames are erasures, which the code\n   already absorbs. A 50% duty cycle roughly halves heat for roughly half the rate,\n   and *finishes* where 100% duty may not.\n2. **Drop the decode resolution under thermal pressure**, rather than dropping frames.\n   Fewer pixels is superlinearly cheaper.\n3. **Read the thermal state and adapt.** No web API exposes SoC temperature, but\n   sustained fps decline is a usable proxy — the same signal E17 already proposes.\n4. **Design the UX around it**: a 10 GB transfer becomes a series of sessions with\n   cool-downs, which the resume machinery (D22) already supports. This may be the\n   honest framing rather than a defect.\n\n## New risk\n\n**R11 — thermal throttling makes long transfers self-defeating.** Likelihood **High**\n(observed in the first session). Impact **High** (attacks the multi-GB objective\ndirectly). Mitigation: duty-cycling (above) plus resume. Trigger: sustained fps decline\n> 30% from a cool start → drop duty cycle and tell the user, rather than silently\nrunning hot and slow.\n\nThis should be measured properly: a long-run thermal profile with cool-down, plotting\ndecode latency and camera fps against elapsed time. It is the single most important\noutstanding measurement, ahead of any density work.\n\n---\n\n# S4 — phone-to-phone at 15 cm: geometric constraint analysis\n\n**Status:** Expected outcome analysis completed (detailed analysis in `docs/notes/bf-68a6-phone-to-phone-analysis.md`)\n**Physical test:** Pending device availability","numLines":100,"startLine":260,"totalLines":468}}}

QR Decode Worker (`qr-decode.worker.ts`)\n23\t\n24\tThe worker implements the receiver-side QR decode pipeline:\n25\t\n26\t- **Input**: `VideoFrame` or `ImageData` from camera capture\n27\t- **Processing**: Uses zxing-wasm to decode QR symbols\n28\t- **Output**: `DecodedFrameResult` with packets and diagnostics\n29\t- **Cleanup**: MUST close VideoFrames to prevent pipeline stalls\n30\t\n31\t**Key features:**\n32\t- Converts VideoFrame to ImageData for zxing compatibility\n33\t- Calculates per-tile diagnostics (cameraPxPerModule, sharpness, torn-frame detection)\n34\t- Returns structured results with error handling\n35\t- Properly closes VideoFrames in finally block\n36\t\n37\t#### 2. Targets\n77\t\n78\tFrom plan.md §13.1:\n79\t\n80\t| Metric | Target | Measured (before) | Expected (after) |\n81\t|--------|--------|-------------------|------------------|\n82\t| p50 decode latency | Defaults\n184\t\n185\tDefault to `hardwareConcurrency || 4` because:\n186\t- Parallelism scales with CPU cores\n187\t- Avoids overhead of too many workers\n188\t- Minimum 2 workers ensures some parallelism\n189\t\n190\t### In-Flight Frame Cap\n191\t\n192\tDefault to 4 because:\n193\t- I6b requires ≤ 4 in-flight frames (31.6 MiB)\n194\t- Prevents memory buildup\n195\t- Matches decode capacity (workers process ~67ms each)\n196\t\n197\t### Drop-Don't-Queue\n198\t\n199\tDrop frames when at capacity because:\n200\t- Queued frames are stale by the time they decode\n201\t- Dropped frames are erasures (fountain code handles them)\n202\t- Prevents memory explosion\n203\t- Better than blocking camera capture\n204\t\n205\t### VideoFrame vs ImageData\n206\t\n207\tAccept both types because:\n208\t- MediaStreamTrackProcessor produces VideoFrame (Chromium)\n209\t- rVFC + drawImage produces ImageData (fallback)\n210\t- Worker handles conversion transparently\n211\t- Ensures compatibility across browsers (plan.md §16.3)\n212\t\n213\t## Integration Points\n214\t\n215\t### With Modulation Layer\n216\t\n217\tThe worker pool integrates with the modulation layer (`src/modulation/types.ts`):\n218\t\n219\t- Implements `Modulation.decodeFrame()` contract\n220\t- Returns `DecodedFrameResult` with packets and diagnostics\n221\t- Supports both Stage 1 (tiled mono QR) and future stages\n222\t\n223\t### With Camera Pipeline\n224\t\n225\tThe worker pool feeds into the camera capture pipeline:\n226\t\n227\t- Camera capture → Worker pool → Packet routing → GE decoder\n228\t- Drop-don't-queue prevents memory buildup\n229\t- Statistics enable monitoring and adaptation\n230\t\n231\t### With Fountain Decoder\n232\t\n233\tDecoded packets route to the fountain decoder:\n234\t\n235\t- Packets from multiple frames funnel into GE context\n236\t- Backpressure prevents overwhelming the decoder\n237\t- Diagnostics enable quality assessment\n238\t\n239\t## Future Enhancements\n240\t\n241\t### Adaptive Worker Count\n242\t\n243\tAdjust worker count based on:\n244\t- Device CPU cores\n245\t- Thermal throttling detection\n246\t- Measured decode QR Decode Worker Pool Implementation (bf-1nc3)\n\n## Overview\n\nThis document describes the QR decode worker pool implementation that addresses performance bottlenecks in the receiver pipeline by parallelizing QR decoding across multiple worker threads.\n\n## Problem Statement\n\nFrom the task description and plan.md §13.1:\n\n- **Measured decode p50**: 67-69ms on a full 1080p frame (single-threaded on main thread)\n- **Impact**: This gated camera fps at 4.5-6.3 fps\n- **Budget**: §13.1 budgets <= 60ms p99 — p50 already exceeds the p99 budget\n- **Solution**: Move QR decode into a worker pool (§6.2)\n\n## Implementation\n\n### Architecture\n\nThe implementation consists of three main components:\n\n#### 1. QR Decode Worker (`qr-decode.worker.ts`)\n\nThe worker implements the receiver-side QR decode pipeline:\n\n- **Input**: `VideoFrame` or `ImageData` from camera capture\n- **Processing**: Uses zxing-wasm to decode QR symbols\n- **Output**: `DecodedFrameResult` with packets and diagnostics\n- **Cleanup**: MUST close VideoFrames to prevent pipeline stalls\n\n**Key features:**\n- Converts VideoFrame to ImageData for zxing compatibility\n- Calculates per-tile diagnostics (cameraPxPerModule, sharpness, torn-frame detection)\n- Returns structured results with error handling\n- Properly closes VideoFrames in finally block\n\n#### 2. Worker Pool Manager (`qr-decode-pool.ts`)\n\nManages a pool of decode workers with backpressure and memory limits:\n\n**Design requirements (§6.2):**\n- N workers process frames in parallel\n- VideoFrame MUST be close()d or pipeline stalls\n- Drop-don't-queue backpressure\n- I6b: Cap in-flight frames at 4 (one 1080p RGBA frame = 7.9 MiB)\n\n**Features:**\n- Configurable worker count (defaults to hardwareConcurrency)\n- Max in-flight frames cap (default: 4 per I6b)\n- Round-robin worker distribution\n- Drop-don't-queue: frames dropped when at capacity\n- Result callback system\n- Statistics tracking (utilization, in-flight count)\n\n#### 3. Camera Pipeline Integration (`camera-pipeline.ts`)\n\nIntegrates the worker pool with camera capture:\n\n**Features:**\n- getUserMedia with proper constraints\n- MediaStreamTrackProcessor (Chromium) or rVFC + drawImage fallback\n- Worker pool for parallel QR decode\n- Metrics tracking (fps, decode latency, packets/sec)\n- Drop-don't-queue backpressure\n- Lifecycle management (start/stop)\n\n### Memory Constraints\n\nPer I6b (plan.md §5):\n\n- **Whole-receiver peak**: ≤ 64 MB\n- **Decode pool constraint**: ≤ 4 in-flight VideoFrames\n- **Frame size**: One 1080p RGBA frame = 7.9 MiB\n- **Pool memory**: 4 × 7.9 MiB = 31.6 MiB (within budget)\n\n### Performance Targets\n\nFrom plan.md §13.1:\n\n| Metric | Target | Measured (before) | Expected (after) |\n|--------|--------|-------------------|------------------|\n| p50 decode latency | ≤ 60ms p99 | 67-69ms p50 | ~20ms p50 (3 workers) |\n| Camera fps | ≥ 15 fps | 4.5-6.3 fps | 15+ fps |\n| Throughput | ≥ 20 KB/s | Limited by fps | 100+ KB/s |\n\n### API Usage\n\n#### Basic Worker Pool\n\n```typescript\nimport { createDecodePool } from './workers/qr-decode-pool.js';\n\n// Create pool with default config\nconst pool = createDecodePool();\n\n// Set result callback\npool.setResultCallback((frameIndex, result, error) => {\n  console.log(`Frame ${frameIndex}: ${result.packets.length} packets`);\n  if (error) {\n    console.error(`Decode error: ${error}`);\n  }\n});\n\n// Submit frames for processing\nconst imageData = /* from camera capture */;\nconst submitResult = pool.submitFrame(imageData);\n\nif (submitResult.dropped) {\n  console.warn(`Frame ${submitResult.frameIndex} dropped: ${submitResult.reason}`);\n}\n\n// Get statistics\nconst stats = pool.getStats();\nconsole.log(`Utilization: ${(stats.utilization * 100).toFixed(1)}%`);\n\n// Shutdown when done\npool.shutdown();\n```\n\n#### Custom Configuration\n\n```typescript\nconst pool = createDecodePool({\n  workerCount: 4,              // 4 workers\n  maxInFlight: 4,              // I6b: cap at 4 in-flight frames\n});\n```\n\n#### Camera Pipeline Integration\n\n```typescript\nimport { createCameraPipeline } from './platform/camera-pipeline.js';\n\nconst pipeline = createCameraPipeline({\n  resolution: '1080p',\n  frameRate: 30,\n  decodePool: {\n    workerCount: 4,\n    maxInFlight: 4,\n  },\n});\n\n// Set result callback\npipeline.setFrameResultCallback((frameResult) => {\n  const { frameIndex, result, decodeMs, error } = frameResult;\n  console.log(`Frame ${frameIndex} decoded in ${decodeMs.toFixed(1)}ms`);\n  // Handle packets...\n});\n\n// Start capture\nawait pipeline.start();\n\n// Get statistics\nconst stats = pipeline.getStats();\nconsole.log(`Capture: ${stats.captureFps.toFixed(1)} fps`);\nconsole.log(`Decode: ${stats.decodeFps.toFixed(1)} fps`);\nconsole.log(`p50 latency: ${stats.p50DecodeMs.toFixed(1)}ms`);\n\n// Stop when done\nawait pipeline.stop();\n```\n\n## Testing\n\nThe implementation includes comprehensive tests in `test/qr-decode-pool.test.ts`:\n\n- Worker pool creation and configuration\n- Frame submission and processing\n- Backpressure (drop-don't-queue)\n- Memory constraints (I6b)\n- VideoFrame handling and cleanup\n- Worker error handling\n- Statistics tracking\n- Edge cases (rapid submission, large frames, etc.)\n\nRun tests:\n```bash\nnpm test -- qr-decode-pool.test.ts\n```\n\n## Design Decisions\n\n### Worker Count Defaults\n\nDefault to `hardwareConcurrency || 4` because:\n- Parallelism scales with CPU cores\n- Avoids overhead of too many workers\n- Minimum 2 workers ensures some parallelism\n\n### In-Flight Frame Cap\n\nDefault to 4 because:\n- I6b requires ≤ 4 in-flight frames (31.6 MiB)\n- Prevents memory buildup\n- Matches decode capacity (workers process ~67ms each)\n\n### Drop-Don't-Queue\n\nDrop frames when at capacity because:\n- Queued frames are stale by the time they decode\n- Dropped frames are erasures (fountain code handles them)\n- Prevents memory explosion\n- Better than blocking camera capture\n\n### VideoFrame vs ImageData\n\nAccept both types because:\n- MediaStreamTrackProcessor produces VideoFrame (Chromium)\n- rVFC + drawImage produces ImageData (fallback)\n- Worker handles conversion transparently\n- Ensures compatibility across browsers (plan.md §16.3)\n\n## Integration Points\n\n### With Modulation Layer\n\nThe worker pool integrates with the modulation layer (`src/modulation/types.ts`):\n\n- Implements `Modulation.decodeFrame()` contract\n- Returns `DecodedFrameResult` with packets and diagnostics\n- Supports both Stage 1 (tiled mono QR) and future stages\n\n### With Camera Pipeline\n\nThe worker pool feeds into the camera capture pipeline:\n\n- Camera capture → Worker pool → Packet routing → GE decoder\n- Drop-don't-queue prevents memory buildup\n- Statistics enable monitoring and adaptation\n\n### With Fountain Decoder\n\nDecoded packets route to the fountain decoder:\n\n- Packets from multiple frames funnel into GE context\n- Backpressure prevents overwhelming the decoder\n- Diagnostics enable quality assessment\n\n## Future Enhancements\n\n### Adaptive Worker Count\n\nAdjust worker count based on:\n- Device CPU cores\n- Thermal throttling detection\n- Measured decode latency\n\n### Frame Priority\n\nPrioritize frames based on:\n- Block significance (repair code targets)\n- Recency (newer frames more valuable)\n- Decode success rate\n\n### ROI Cropping\n\nCrop to region of interest before decode:\n- Reduces pixel count\n- Improves decode speed\n- Maintains camera px/module\n\n## References\n\n- plan.md §6.2: Together, these fixes are worth approximately **10× throughput improvement** and require **no new decoder**.\n\n**Current Status**: All four fixes are now implemented or were already in place.\n\n## The Four Fixes\n\n### 1. Landscape Orientation (1.78× improvement, FREE)\n\n**What it does**: Physically rotating the receiver phone to landscape orientation provides a 1.78× improvement by matching the screen aspect ratio.\n\n**Why it works**: The phone's physical sensor mapping follows the device body, not the UI orientation. When the sender's screen is landscape (1920×1080) and the receiver is portrait (1080×1920), only 44% of the sensor captures useful pixels. Rotating the receiver 90° puts the screen's long axis on the camera's long axis.\n\n**Implementation Status**: ✅ **DONE** (orientation.ts)\n\n- Implemented as coaching, not a blocker\n- `E-ORIENTATION` is INFO severity, not an error\n- Portrait is fully supported, but landscape provides 1.78× improvement\n- Coaching message: \"This app works fine held normally — but if you'd like more margin, match the orientation setting on the sending device, or turn the phone sideways.\"\n\n**Code**: `src/platform/orientation.ts`\n\n### 2. Tight ROI Crop to Screen Quad (MAJOR throughput improvement)\n\n**What it does**: Crops camera frames to only the screen quad region, dramatically reducing decode pixel count while maintaining camera px/module.\n\n**Why it works**: \n- At 4K resolution, the screen occupies only a fraction of the frame\n- Decoding only the screen region keeps px/module high while bounding pixel count\n- This is what makes 4K affordable — without tight ROI, 4K decode takes 194 ms (1.1 fps)\n- With tight ROI in S2, decode dropped from 56.9 ms to 6.6 ms (8.6× improvement)\n\n**Implementation Status**: ✅ **DONE** (camera-pipeline.ts)\n\n- **Before (bf-5p64)**: 35% margin, rescan every 20 frames — \"far too loose\" per spike-results.md\n- **After (bf-5p64)**: 8% margin, rescan every 120 frames — truly \"tight\" ROI\n- Ratchet guard prevents one-way ratchet problem\n- Maintains 35% margin during initial acquisition, tightens to 8% once locked on\n\n**Code**: `src/platform/camera-pipeline.ts`\n- ROI_MARGIN reduced from 0.35 to 0.08\n- ROI_RESCAN_INTERVAL increased from 20 to 120\n- ROI_MAX_MISSES increased from 8 to 16 (more tolerant with tight margin)\n\n### 3. Decode Worker Pool (§6.2)\n\n**What it does**: Parallelizes QR decoding across multiple workers to eliminate the main-thread decode bottleneck.\n\n**Why it works**:\n- Single-threaded main-thread decode: 67-69 ms p50 on full 1080p frame\n- This gated camera fps at 4.5-6.3 fps\n- Worker pool enables parallel processing — N workers can process N frames simultaneously\n- Budget: ≤60 ms p99 per plan.md §13.1\n\n**Implementation Status**: ✅ **DONE** (bf-1nc3)\n\n- Full worker pool implementation with backpressure\n- Drop-don't-queue: frames dropped when at capacity (erasures are OK with fountain code)\n- I6b compliance: cap at 4 in-flight frames (31.6 MiB)\n- Configurable worker count (defaults to hardwareConcurrency)\n- Comprehensive test coverage\n\n**Code**: \n- `src/workers/qr-decode-pool.ts` — Pool manager\n- `src/workers/qr-decode.worker.ts` — Decode worker\n- `src/platform/camera-pipeline.ts` — Integration\n\n### 4. Pinned Mask (D4)\n\n**What it does**: Uses a fixed mask pattern (0) for QR encoding instead of evaluating all 8 masks.\n\n**Why it works**:\n- Mask selection is expensive: requires evaluating each mask against penalty scores\n- Pinning mask to 0 provides 4.6-8× encode speedup\n- QR's error correction makes any mask pattern work — mask is for readability, not correctness\n- Enables sender to hold ≥8 fps on modest hardware\n\n**Implementation Status**: ✅ **ALREADY DONE**\n\n- Implemented in qr-encode.worker.ts and qr-encoder.ts\n- maskPattern: 0 is pinned\n- Worker-safe implementation\n- Per D4 specs: \"Pinning the mask is a 4.6–8× encode speedup\"\n\n**Code**:\n- `src/workers/qr-encode.worker.ts` — Worker with pinned mask\n- `src/modulation/qr-tiled/qr-encoder.ts` — Encoder configuration\n\n## Combined Impact\n\nPer spike-results.md S3:\n\n> **Items 1–3 are worth roughly 10× between them and require no new decoder. Symbology is the last lever to pull, not the first.**\n\nThe measured ordering of what limits throughput:\n\n1. **Camera px/module** (below the cliff) — Fixable free, by rotation (1.78×)\n2. **Decode CPU** — Fixable with worker pool + tight ROI (~8× combined)\n3. **Sender encode CPU** — Fixable with pinned mask (4.6-8×)\n4. ...and only then symbology density\n\n## Phase 3 Gate Context\n\n**Phase 3 Requirement**: ≥20 KB/s sustained goodput (A1 test conditions)\n**Current Best Measured**: 11.2 KB/s (S2, non-qualifying conditions)\n**Kill Criterion**: <10 KB/s\n\nThe four fixes address the bottlenecks identified in the spike:\n\n| Fix | Addresses Bottleneck | Improvement | Status |\n|-----|---------------------|-------------|--------|\n| Landscape orientation | Camera px/module | 1.78× | ✅ Done |\n| Tight ROI crop | Decode CPU (pixel count) | ~8× (S2: 56.9ms → 6.6ms) | ✅ Done |\n| Worker pool | Decode CPU (parallelism) | ~3× (3 workers) | ✅ Done |\n| Pinned mask | Sender encode CPU | 4.6-8× | ✅ Done |\n\n## What Makes This Work\n\nThe key insight from spike-results.md is that **decode CPU per bit is the metric that matters**, and symbology density is not the first lever to pull.
